title: What caused all this?
hookLine: a circle of seekers weighs time, fate and chance as the cause of everything, and finds one Lord behind them
carry: one lord behind time, fate and chance
last: THE KNOWER GOES HOME, LIKE RIVERS TO THE SEA.

lines: WHY DID THINGS TURN OUT THIS WAY?
cards: Why did things turn out this way? People ask it after a near miss on the highway, after a diagnosis, after meeting someone on a train they almost didn't catch. And they reach for answers.
It was just timing. That's how I am. It was meant to be.

Pure luck. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens with thinkers asking the same thing about the whole world, and it lines up the very same answers: time, nature, fate, chance. Then it does something brave.
It says none of these is enough.

teach.h: WHAT IS THE CAUSE? WHO GOVERNS US?
teach.b: It opens with the brahmavadins, people who talk about Brahman, in discussion. What is the cause? Is it Brahman?
Where are we born from? Who governs us as we move through pleasure and pain? Then the candidates.
Kala, time: everything ripens and rots on its own schedule. Svabhava, inborn nature: fire is hot because that's what fire is. Niyati, necessity, fixed law, fate.
Yadriccha, chance. The elements. The womb.
The person, purusha. Should one of these be the cause? The text takes each one seriously.

Then the verdict: not any one of them, and not even all of them combined, because there's a self here too, and the self on its own isn't master of its pleasure and pain either. So the seekers stop arguing.
They turn to meditation and yoga, and in meditation they see the power of God, hidden by its own qualities, the one who rules over all those causes, from time to the self.
That's the big claim, and a lasting Hindu belief: behind time, nature, fate and chance stands one Lord, Ishvara, who holds them all.

teach.h: NONE ALONE; NOT EVEN ALL COMBINED.
teach.b: It's why, after a near miss on the road, a Hindu grandmother may skip the word lucky and go light a lamp at the home shrine to say thank you.

teach.h: IN MEDITATION, THE POWER OF GOD.
teach.b: This Upanishad later names that Lord Rudra; Shaiva traditions hold it dear.
Tomorrow, the seekers describe what they saw: a wheel.

how: The Shvetashvatara is studied across Vedanta schools and has a special place in Shaiva traditions, which honor its praise of Rudra-Shiva as the Lord who rules over time and all other causes.

o: a chariot wheel offered in the fire rite
a great wheel in which everything lives and rests
the cycle of chance that rules every life

s: the Shvetashvatara picks time as the true cause
none alone, not even all combined, is enough.

in meditation they see the power of God, who rules all those causes.
this Upanishad speaks of God as a personal Lord

games.q: you're in the circle of seekers. time, nature, fate, chance: none of them explains the world. what do you do, and what do you find?
o: pick the likeliest and move on.
turn to meditation and yoga, and look.
decide the question has no answer.
games.why: they practice dhyana-yoga, and see the power of God, hidden in its own qualities, who rules every cause from time to the self.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that happened to you that you can't fully explain, good or hard. Notice the answer you usually reach for: timing, temperament, fate or luck, and hold it loosely.
Then do what the seekers did: stop arguing and sit with it.
If you pray, offer it to the one they saw ruling every cause, the way many Hindus give thanks at the home shrine; if you don't, let the question rest in the quiet while you breathe beside it.

wordCard.voice: Brahmacakra, the wheel of Brahman. The Shvetashvatara opens by asking what is the cause, time, nature, necessity, chance, and finds no single answer enough, until the seekers turn to meditation.

orig.note: Sanskrit brahmacakra, the wheel of Brahman: the vast wheel of Shvetashvatara 1.6, in which all things live and rest.

carryVoice: Your line: one Lord behind time, fate and chance. The seekers found him in meditation. Day four hundred twenty-one.
